content_voiceover: This slide covers the clinical presentation of neuroblastoma, which can be dramatic because of its tendency to secrete catecholamines and metastasize early. Local symptoms depend on the primary site, an abdominal mass if it arises from the adrenal gland or paraspinal ganglia, or a chest mass if it arises in the posterior mediastinum, sometimes causing bone pain from local invasion. A paraspinal cervical or thoracic tumor can compress the sympathetic chain and cause Horner syndrome, remembered by the tetrad of myosis, or a constricted pupil, ptosis, or a droopy eyelid, enophthalmos, a sunken eye, and anhydrosis, or loss of sweating on that side of the face. Because most children present with metastatic disease at diagnosis, fellows should also recognize the systemic features, irritability, weight loss, bone pain from marrow or skeletal metastases, fever, proptosis, and periorbital ecchymoses, often called raccoon eyes, from metastasis to the orbital bones. Anemia is also common and is typically normochromic and normocytic, reflecting marrow infiltration.
keypoints: Local mass effect, abdominal or chest lump, depending on primary site
Horner syndrome, myosis, ptosis, enophthalmos, anhydrosis
Raccoon eyes, periorbital ecchymoses from orbital bone metastasis
Metastatic features, irritability, weight loss, bone pain, fever, proptosis
Normochromic normocytic anemia from marrow infiltration
keypoint_voiceover: Two exam findings are classic exam-question triggers. Horner syndrome, myosis, ptosis, enophthalmos, and anhydrosis, points to a cervical or thoracic paraspinal tumor compressing the sympathetic chain. And raccoon eyes, periorbital ecchymosis, points to metastatic disease infiltrating the orbital bones. Add in irritability, weight loss, bone pain, fever, and a normochromic normocytic anemia, and you have the classic picture of metastatic neuroblastoma at presentation.
